narration: Even a spotless window pane reflects about 8 percent of the light striking it.

heading: Cold open
narration: That loss is real, and it is almost the only loss. Glass is clear because visible light does not carry enough energy to excite the electrons held in its silicon and oxygen bonds, so the light passes through instead of being absorbed.

heading: Cold open

heading: Cold open
narration: The answer overturns a common assumption. Glass does not do something special to become transparent. It simply fails to stop the light.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter
narration: Not absorbing light is necessary, but it is not enough. A material can refuse to absorb light and still be opaque, because it scatters the light instead.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter
narration: Table salt is a good example. A single large crystal of salt is clear.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter
narration: Grind it and you get a white powder, even though nothing chemical has changed.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter
narration: Every surface between grains bends and reflects a little light. After thousands of those surfaces, the light has been sent in every direction. White is what scattered, unabsorbed light looks like.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter
narration: Aluminium oxide shows the same effect in a much harder material. As a single crystal sapphire, it is clear, which is why it is used for watch faces.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter
narration: As an ordinary polycrystalline ceramic, it is white. That form is made of countless tiny grains with pores between them.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter
narration: The ceramics literature from ASM International treats this as a standard case.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter
narration: Making a ceramic transparent depends on removing pores and controlling grain boundaries. The chemistry stays the same.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter
narration: Glass avoids this problem because it has no grains at all. It is amorphous, meaning its atoms have no repeating long-range order.

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter

heading: Disorder is why glass does not scatter

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: Look at the edge of a sheet of ordinary window glass, and it is green.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: Look through the face, and you barely notice any tint. Both views show the same material, but the edge gives the light a much longer path.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: The green comes from iron, which is present as a trace impurity in sand and other raw materials.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: Unlike the silica around them, iron ions do have electronic transitions in the visible range.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: They absorb a little of the red end of the spectrum and a little of the blue.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: Over a few millimetres, the effect is faint. Along the length of the edge, it is obvious.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: Manufacturers sell low-iron glass for display cases and solar panels specifically to remove that tint.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: This is why the history of glass is largely a history of chemistry.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: Ancient glassmakers could not buy pure sand, and much early glass is tinted or deeply coloured.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: Collections such as the British Museum's hold Roman vessels that were made nearly colourless.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: Their makers added compounds of manganese or antimony to counteract the tint of iron.

heading: Colour in glass comes from what was added, not from silica
narration: Cobalt gave a deep blue, and copper gave turquoise and red. In each case, colour in glass came from trace impurities and added metals, not from the silica network, which stays clear underneath.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: This evidence explains why silica-based glass transmits visible light. It does not give a complete atomic picture of glass.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: The arrangement of atoms in an amorphous solid cannot be read directly the way a crystal structure can.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: It has to be inferred from scattering experiments and computer simulations, and the models still differ in detail.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: A general explanation also cannot tell you the losses of any given pane.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: Iron content, thickness, coatings and surface condition all vary, and the published figures for one product do not transfer to another.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: The settled parts are why visible light is not absorbed and why glass does not scatter.

heading: Evidence limit
narration: The exact structure of glass remains an open and active research question.

heading: Closing
narration: Glass is clear for a modest reason. Across the visible range, glass absorbs almost nothing, scatters almost nothing, and reflects a little at each face.

heading: Closing
narration: Everything you see through a window is light the glass failed to stop.
